source_text: Περὶ τῆς ξηρανθείσης συκῆς. Ὁ Μάρκος προστίθησιν ὅτι μακρόθεν ἰδὼν συκῆν ἔχουσαν φύλλα ἦλθεν εἰ ἄρα τι εὑρήσει ἐν αὐτῇ· καὶ μηδὲν εὑρὼν εἰ μὴ φύλλα μόνον (οὐ γὰρ ἦν καιρὸς σύκων) εἶπεν· «Μηκέτι εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα ἐκ σοῦ μηδεὶς καρπὸν φάγῃ.» Οἱ τοῦ πνεύματος καρποὶ — ἀγάπη, χαρά, εἰρήνη, μακροθυμία, χρηστότης, ἀγαθωσύνη, πίστις, πραΰτης, ἐγκράτεια — ποτὲ μὲν ἐν οἰκείοις ἀποδίδονται καιροῖς· βέλτιον δὲ εἰ καίπερ τῶν περιστάσεων ἐπὶ τοὐναντίον τῇ καρποφορίᾳ προκαλουμένων δυνηθείη τις διὰ τὸ πάνυ ὠφελεῖσθαι ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου οὐδὲν ἧττον καὶ τότε φέρειν τοὺς καρπούς. Εἶπε δὲ ὁ Ἰησοῦς τοῖς μαθηταῖς· «Αἰτεῖτε τὰ μεγάλα, καὶ τὰ μικρὰ προστεθήσεται ὑμῖν· καὶ αἰτεῖτε τὰ ἐπουράνια, καὶ τὰ ἐπίγεια προστεθήσεται ὑμῖν.»
thought_title: The withered fig tree and the fruit of the Spirit
orientation: Origen is commenting on the Gospel account of Jesus cursing the fig tree, and he now explains the spiritual meaning of the tree's lack of fruit.
pass_a_gloss: Concerning the withered fig tree. Mark adds that, having seen from afar a fig tree having leaves, he came, if perhaps he would find something on it; and having found nothing except leaves only (for it was not the season of figs), he said: 'No longer forever may anyone eat fruit from you.' The fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control — is at one time rendered in its proper seasons; but it is better if, even though circumstances are urging the opposite to fruit-bearing, someone might be able, because of being greatly benefited by the word, no less even then to bear the fruits. And Jesus said to the disciples: 'Ask for the great things, and the small things will be added to you; and ask for the heavenly things, and the earthly things will be added to you.'

choices.why: The section heading uses the aorist passive participle to name the event; 'withered' preserves the passive force and the standard English rendering of the Gospel episode.
The glossary gives 'fruit of the Spirit' for fructus spiritus; the plural here matches the list that follows and the Pauline source.

choices.english: are rendered in their proper seasons
choices.why: The middle voice of ἀποδίδονται suggests the fruits are given back or yielded at the times that belong to them; 'proper seasons' keeps the sense of fitting or appropriate times.
rejected: are given in their own times
are produced at their own seasons

choices.why: The neuter plural substantive is kept as a substantive in English to preserve the contrast with 'the small things' and 'the heavenly things' and 'the earthly things.'
The future passive of προστίθημι is rendered literally to preserve the promise form and the dative of advantage.
rejected: will be given to you as well

pass_b_english: On the withered fig tree. Mark adds that when Jesus saw a fig tree with leaves from a distance, he went to see whether he would find anything on it. Finding nothing but leaves only—for it was not the season for figs—he said, “May no one ever eat fruit from you again” (Mark 11:13-14). The fruit of the Spirit—love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control (Galatians 5:22-23)—is sometimes produced in its proper seasons. But it is better if, even when circumstances press in the opposite direction against fruit-bearing, someone is able, because of being greatly helped by the word, to bear the fruits no less even then. And Jesus said to the disciples, “Ask for the great things, and the small things will be added to you; and ask for the heavenly things, and the earthly things will be added to you.”

problems.source_quote: ποτὲ μὲν ἐν οἰκείοις ἀποδίδονται καιροῖς
problems.why: 'Rendered' suggests external giving; Greek means fruits are produced/yielded in proper seasons.
problems.fix: are sometimes produced in their proper seasons
problems.ruling: ἀποδίδονται means 'yielded/produced' here; 'rendered' misleads about fruit production vs external giving.

edits.old: is sometimes rendered in its proper seasons
edits.new: is sometimes produced in its proper seasons

fixed: Changed 'rendered' to 'produced' because the Greek ἀποδίδονται means the fruits are yielded or produced in their proper seasons, not externally rendered.

last_rejected.source_quote: εἶπεν· «Μηκέτι εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα ἐκ σοῦ μηδεὶς καρπὸν φάγῃ.»
last_rejected.why: English adds "May" making it a wish; Greek is a command/prophetic decree.
last_rejected.fix: "No one shall ever eat fruit from you again."
last_rejected.ruling: Greek μηκέτι...μηδεὶς φάγῃ is a 3rd person subjunctive prohibition; 'May no one' correctly renders it.

last_rejected.quote: because of being greatly helped by the word
last_rejected.source_quote: διὰ τὸ πάνυ ὠφελεῖσθαι ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου
last_rejected.why: "greatly helped" reverses agency; Greek is passive "being benefited," not active "helped."
last_rejected.fix: through being greatly benefited by the word
last_rejected.ruling: ὠφελεῖσθαι is passive 'being benefited/helped'; 'helped' is within normal range, no agency reversal.

last_rejected.source_quote: ποτὲ μὲν ἐν οἰκείοις ἀποδίδονται καιροῖς
last_rejected.why: "is produced" passive misses that fruits are given/rendered (ἀποδίδονται) in due seasons.
last_rejected.fix: are sometimes rendered in their proper seasons
last_rejected.ruling: ἀποδίδονται can mean 'produced/yielded'; 'is produced' is within normal range, not a major error.
